description: Un particular equipo formado por Ingeniería de Sistemas, Economía y Administración se ha unido con una única meta: Ganar. Un grupo como muchos, pero un equipo como pocos, se ha alineado con el objetivo de Ganar Conocimiento, y dentro de lo poco de nuestras vidas intentar hacer algo relevante por el mundo, no solo con una intención, sino también con nuestras habilidades, conocimientos y acción. Nosotros somo CcapoSpace.
summary:
Humanity has left rovers, landers, and probes on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. They finished their missions and remained there, but their stories—and the difficult decisions made by their teams—live on in technical archives that children and young people never see.

Detectives of Other Worlds is a free, bilingual educational website (Spanish and English) that turns 16 of these abandoned machines into cases to solve. Players find each machine through mission maps and photos, face the same decisions as the original teams, and uncover its history: what it achieved, why it stayed, and how it stands today.

The experience is tailored to every age: 8-bit animated stories for those under 14, a search and decision-making game for ages 14 to 17, and a collection of dossiers with classroom questions for teachers. It requires no registration and collects no personal data, making it perfectly safe for classroom use.

Our goal is to keep these stories alive and use them to spark the curiosity that leads to STEM careers. From one question to the universe.
details:
What does it do?

  • Presents 16 machines left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space, from Surveyor 3 (1967) to Ingenuity (2024).
    1. Find it: Search for the machine on a 3D globe and in mission maps or photographs, using clues and a hot-and-cold indicator.
    2. Decide: 32 real-world decisions (2 per case). Players are presented with the situation and what was known at the time. They choose an option, rate their confidence, and compare their decision with what the actual team did. There is no “right” or “wrong” answer: the experience explains why the alternative option also made sense.
    3. Its story: The machine tells its story: what it discovered, why it was left behind, and what its current condition is. Each story includes a photograph, a fact sheet, and source references.
  • Offers a different experience for each age group: 8-bit stories (under 14), a game with three difficulty levels (ages 14–17), and a teacher resource archive with printable case files (ages 18 and older).

How does it work?

  • It is a web application that runs in the browser. When users enter, a neutral welcome screen asks for their age range and prior knowledge to recommend an appropriate level.
  • The 16 cases are stored in a JSON data file that the server delivers along with the webpage. No database is required.
  • User profiles and progress (completed cases and stars) are stored exclusively in the user's browser using localStorage. No data is sent back to the server.
  • The 8-bit animations are rendered in the browser using our own animation engine. Music and sound effects are generated in real time using Web Audio. There are no audio files or external services.
  • Teachers can install it on their computer or on their school's network and use it without relying on third-party services.

Benefits

  • Brings to light real mission stories that are largely unknown, directly addressing the challenge's objectives.
  • Teaches users to think like an engineering team: make decisions with incomplete information, assess risks, and learn from the outcomes.
  • Sparks interest in STEM careers through an engaging format adapted to different age groups.
  • Safe for minors: no registration, no accounts, no analytics, and no personal data collection. The only information visible to the server is the user's IP address, as with any website.
  • Accessible: works on mobile devices, supports screen readers, and includes a reduced-motion mode.
  • Useful for teachers: includes case files with classroom discussion questions, ready to print.

Scope

  • Current version: 16 cases verified against NASA sources, 8 8-bit stories, and 32 decisions, available in Spanish and English.
  • Target audience: Children and young people aged 10–17, teachers, and families in Peru, Latin America, and the United States.
  • Next steps: Add more cases (including missions from other space agencies), develop grade-specific teacher guides, and conduct pilot tests in schools.
  • Sustainability: Free for students, with licensing and educational materials available for schools.

Tools and software used

  • CodeIgniter 4.7 (PHP 8.2), with no database.
  • JavaScript without frameworks.
  • Three.js (3D globes) and OpenSeadragon (zooming in on high-resolution images).
  • Canvas (custom 8-bit animation engine) and Web Audio API (music and sound effects generated in the browser).
  • canvas-confetti; Pixelify Sans, Bricolage Grotesque, and Lexend fonts, all served from the same website.
  • Python (data verification and Solar System model generation), Playwright (automated testing and screenshots), and FFmpeg (video production).
  • Server running CloudPanel (Nginx); source code hosted on GitHub under the MIT License.
